metaDescription: Learn how to exit a TradingView trade in parts, adjusting quantity and setting multiple targets to lock in profits and manage risk gradually.
intro: Closing a position in parts, rather than all at once, lets you lock in profits gradually and manage risk more precisely instead of betting everything on one exit price. This guide covers using TradingView's on-chart order line and the Paper Trading panel to scale out of a position, adjust quantity mid-trade, and set take-profit and stop-loss levels that apply to what's left open. The examples here use a simulated Paper Trading account on a crypto pair, but the same order-line controls apply whether you're connected to a live broker or practicing first.

steps.heading: Open a position and find the order line on your chart
steps.body: Once you're in a trade, TradingView draws a horizontal line across your chart at the entry price with a small toolbar attached — TP and SL buttons for take-profit and stop-loss, a quantity box showing your current position size, and an X to close it entirely. This line is your main control surface for managing the trade without leaving the chart, and it's the same interface whether the position came from a live broker connection or a Paper Trading account.

image.caption: An open position's order line on the chart, showing TP and SL buttons, a quantity field, and a close (X) control.

steps.heading: Edit the quantity to scale out
steps.body: Click into the quantity field on the order line and change the number to less than your full position size, then confirm — this closes exactly that portion of your position at the current market price while leaving the remainder open. In one example here the quantity field shows 22 units with additional controls next to it, including what functions as a delete or adjust action, letting you resize the position directly from the chart rather than opening a separate order form.

image.caption: The order line's quantity field being adjusted, with additional controls next to it for modifying or closing part of the position.

steps.heading: Set take-profit and stop-loss for what remains
steps.body: After scaling out of part of a position, the TP and SL levels attached to the order line apply to whatever quantity is still open, so revisit them once you've partially closed. Dragging the TP line to a new price sets a limit order that will close the remaining position automatically if it's hit, while the SL line does the same on the downside — this is how you set up a second or third target without manually watching the chart for each one.

steps.heading: Use the Paper Trading panel to track positions and orders
steps.body: The Paper Trading panel at the bottom of the screen, next to Pine Editor, Strategy Tester, and Replay Trading, shows your account's Balance, Equity, Realized and Unrealized P&L, and margin figures at a glance, with a Positions tab listing every open trade. Placing or adjusting an order also shows up here as a ticket — for example a Buy order with its own Stop, TP, and SL fields — so you can confirm a partial close registered correctly instead of relying on the chart alone.

image.caption: The Paper Trading panel, showing account balance and margin figures alongside an order ticket with Stop, TP, and SL fields.

steps.heading: Decide between manual exits and limit orders
steps.body: You can manage partial exits two ways: manually, by watching price action and adjusting the quantity field yourself when conditions change, or automatically, by setting multiple limit orders in advance at different price levels so portions of the position close without you needing to be at the screen. Automated limit orders suit a defined plan with clear targets, while manual scaling suits a trade where you want to react to how price is actually behaving.

steps.heading: Know the limits if you're on Paper Trading
steps.body: Paper Trading is a simulated environment, and some brokers' partial-close mechanics don't translate perfectly into the simulation — order behavior around partial fills can differ slightly from what a live broker connection would do. If you're testing a scaling-out strategy before going live, treat the Paper Trading results as directionally useful rather than an exact match, and confirm the mechanics again once connected to a real broker.

faq.question: Can I close only part of a position on TradingView?
faq.answer: Yes — edit the quantity field on the position's order line on the chart, or adjust it from the order ticket, to exit a smaller amount than your full position.

faq.question: Does partial closing work with paper trading?
faq.answer: It works, but Paper Trading is simulated and partial-fill mechanics can behave slightly differently than a live broker connection, so treat results as directionally useful rather than exact.

faq.question: Can I set multiple profit targets for one trade?
faq.answer: Yes — after scaling out of part of a position, you can drag the TP line to a new price for the remainder, effectively setting a new target for what's left open.

faq.question: Is partial closing useful for volatile markets?
faq.answer: Yes, it helps manage risk and lock in gains gradually, which is especially useful when trading volatile crypto or forex markets.

faq.question: Where do I see my current position size and P&L?
faq.answer: The Paper Trading panel at the bottom of the screen shows Account Balance, Equity, Realized and Unrealized P&L, and a Positions tab listing every open trade.
